articles.title: Cboe and Citadel Securities Are Suing to Overturn the CFTC's Approval of Stock Perpetual Futures. Could That Slow Hyperliquid? - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.summary: Cboe and Citadel Securities Are Suing to Overturn the CFTC's Approval of Stock Perpetual Futures. Could That Slow Hyperliquid?  24/7 Wall St.
articles.full_text:
Cboe and Citadel Securities filed a lawsuit hours after regulators greenlighted stock perpetual futures for U.S. exchanges, putting billions in potential trading volume in legal limbo and raising questions about whether Hyperliquid's offshore advantage just got bigger.
Cboe Global Markets (CBOE: CBOE | CBOE Price Prediction) and Citadel Securities are suing to challenge the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) approval of stock perpetual futures, which Hyperliquid (CRYPTO: HYPE) already lists outside the U.S. On November 3, 2026, Cboe joined the Capital Markets Alliance, a group that includes Citadel Securities and the Healthy Markets Association. The alliance filed the lawsuit in a New York federal court just hours after the CFTC chairman cleared these contracts for trading.
Stock perpetual futures, or “perps,” are leveraged contracts that track stock prices and do not expire. Traders in these contracts exchange small, regular payments to keep prices close to the underlying stock price. The lawsuit seeks to overturn the CFTC’s approval, classify these contracts as security-based swaps, and halt trading while the case is being reviewed.
Despite the legal disputes, Hyperliquid’s token has shown little reaction. HYPE is trading at $86, down 1.3% over the past 24 hours but up 7.4% over the past week, sitting about 12% below its all-time high. So, could a lawsuit targeting U.S. exchanges slow down a decentralized exchange like Hyperliquid, which operates outside them?
What Cboe and Citadel Are Asking a New York Court to Undo
CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said on November 3 that stock perps could potentially trade for the first time on CFTC-registered exchanges also authorized by the SEC to handle security futures. He said these new products would give Americans regulated alternatives, rather than forcing them to turn to offshore, often unregulated venues.
The plaintiffs’ core argument turns on definitions. A futures contract promises delivery on a specific date, while a perp has no expiration date and does not culminate in an actual delivery. The plaintiffs argue that without an expiry, only cash payments based on the stock’s price remain, which fits the legal definition of a security-based swap.
This classification determines who can sell these financial products. Under the Dodd-Frank Act, retail investors may buy security-based swaps only on fully registered securities exchanges, and only with an SEC-approved disclosure document. If the court agrees with the plaintiffs’ classification, CFTC-regulated exchanges would not be able to offer stock perps to retail traders.
The lawsuit also questions the approval process itself. In September, Coinbase (NASDAQ: COIN), Bitnomial, and another CFTC-registered exchange submitted applications for stock perps. CFTC rules state that a product is considered approved if the agency does not object within 45 days. The CFTC raised no objections and issued no written order. A spokesperson said markets should operate under the rule of law, rather than be stymied by litigation.
What Cboe and Citadel Stand to Lose if Stock Perps Take Off
Both Cboe and Citadel have commercial interests in this matter. Cboe reported net revenue of $469.5 million in its options business for the third quarter, a 23% increase driven by record trading in zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options, which expire the same day they are traded. The firm estimates that retail investors made up 58% of the S&P 500 index’s 0DTE volume, marking them as a key audience for stock perps.
Free Report, Just Released
Why Didn't CBOE Make The Top 10 List?
24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now. Not the ten biggest companies. Not the ten everyone is arguing about. The ten best stocks to buy right now.
And CBOE didn't make the cut!
The report is free, and you can see why we think each stock is a top investment today.
As a private market maker, Citadel Securities profits from continuously quoting buy and sell prices across stocks and options on SEC-regulated platforms. Thus, the investor-protection messages from both firms may partly stem from concerns about losing trading volume to stock perps.
Cboe CEO Craig Donohue voiced concerns during an earnings call on October 30, suggesting that with perpetual futures, “losses are unbounded and positions may get liquidated quickly if market conditions turn,” while simultaneously endorsing the options that Cboe offers.
He did mention “things like perpetuals” as potential products for Cboe Clear U.S., suggesting that Cboe’s opposition may stem partly from a contest over which regulator oversees the product.
Why the Lawsuit Would Slow Hyperliquid’s U.S. Rivals First
Selig’s approval is specific to CFTC-registered exchanges, and since Hyperliquid does not fall under this category, the lawsuit would first affect U.S. applicants like Coinbase and Bitnomial. If a judge halts trading, Hyperliquid’s offshore stock perps might face fewer regulated U.S. competitors in the short term.
However, Hyperliquid’s U.S. plans operate within the framework the lawsuit disputes. Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE: ICE), the parent company of the NYSE, has agreed to be “the exclusive operator of Trade XYZ’s regulated markets” and to invest in the company. Trade XYZ aims to develop perps on stocks and other traditional assets on Hyperliquid’s blockchain.
As ICE CEO Jeff Sprecher stated on October 29, “we need regulatory approval and to see what the CFTC is willing to allow.”
The lawsuit focuses solely on single-stock contracts, which limits its overall impact. As Sprecher pointed out, “at the moment, perpetual contracts are largely crypto-related,” indicating that a win for the plaintiffs could hinder the stock aspect of ICE’s plans, while crypto-related perps may continue as usual. ICE is not part of the lawsuit and has not publicly taken a position.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Midterm Results Are Unlikely to Trigger U-Turn in Treasury Yields – 'Trump Keeps the Final Say,' Analyst Says - TradingView
articles.summary: EXCLUSIVE: Midterm Results Are Unlikely to Trigger U-Turn in Treasury Yields – 'Trump Keeps the Final Say,' Analyst Says  TradingView
articles.full_text:
A new story is spreading across Wall Street on Wednesday: the midterm elections were good news for bonds.
The logic is simple. A Democratic-led Congress can block President Donald Trump‘s expansionary fiscal bills, restraining Washington’s spending and, with it, the flood of new Treasury bond supply that has pushed yields to multi-decade highs.
Not everyone is buying it.
“The only real avenue from the midterms that could conceivably trigger a sustained dollar decline, as we see it, is if the Democrats are successful in pressuring Trump to end the Iran war early, thus triggering a move lower in oil prices and a reversal in safe haven flows,” Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at Ebury, told Benzinga in an exclusive interview Wednesday.
“But ending the war would need Republican help and Trump keeps the final say, so a deal would more likely come from him than from Congress,” he added.
In other words, the key to lower yields does not sit on Capitol Hill. It sits in the Oval Office.
Treasuries Rallied, But Yields Are Still Well Above January Levels
Bonds did catch a bid after Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate.
The 10-year Treasury yield fell 4.7 basis points to 4.92% Wednesday, while the 2-year yield slipped 3.5 basis points to 4.60%. The 30-year yield eased 3.3 basis points to 5.30%.
Still, the relief barely dents the year’s damage.
Ten-year yields started 2026 near 4.19%, which means they are still up about 73 basis points this year. The 2-year yield has climbed more than 110 basis points from about 3.49%, a sign that markets have been repricing the Federal Reserve rather than Washington’s deficit alone.
The iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF TLT rose 0.4% Wednesday, but it remains down about 7% in 2026. Meanwhile, the U.S. Dollar Index fell 0.5% to 101.35.
Why Gridlock Is a Brake, Not a Reversal
Ryan’s skepticism starts with the veto.
Democrats are unlikely to reach the two-thirds Senate majority needed to override Trump. As a result, they can stop new tax cuts and spending, but the measures already in place stay.
“Congress can block new spending but cannot unwind what is already in place,” Ryan said in emailed comments earlier Wednesday. He added that the real fiscal test will come with the debt-ceiling negotiations in 2027.
The result was also no surprise. Prediction markets had priced a probability above 90% that Democrats would flip the House and above 70% that they would take the Senate as well, according to Ebury’s post-election report.
Oil, Not Congress, Is the Real Swing Factor for Yields
For Ryan, high yields are more a byproduct of energy prices than of fiscal policy.
West Texas Intermediate crude fell 3.0% to $93.22 a barrel Wednesday, while Brent dropped 2.8% to $100.65. Both are still up more than 60% this year.
That keeps inflation expectations elevated. Consequently, bond investors are reluctant to accept lower yields.
“With the Iran war ongoing, we see limited pullback in yields in the near-term, both in the US and globally, which should both keep US assets attractive due to rate differentials and support safe haven flows into the greenback,” Ryan said.
A Democratic Congress could increase pressure on the White House to end the conflict. However, it cannot dictate U.S. military or foreign policy, according to Ryan.
Who Wins If Bond Markets Calm Down?
Ryan still sees one route to a softer dollar.
“That said, any signs that trading in bond markets is becoming more orderly could be bearish for the dollar, and we would expect higher-yielding emerging market currencies to be the main beneficiaries of the move,” he said.
The iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF (NYSE:EEM) is up about 9% this year.
The Senate result also matters for the Fed. Every nominee to the central bank’s board needs Senate confirmation, so Democrats can now slow Trump’s push for governors who favor lower rates.
“At the margins, we think that the Democratic win in the Senate should allay Fed independence fears, though the impact in reality is small given few governor positions will actually be available between now and the end of Trump’s term,” Ryan said.
Congress can slow the supply of new bonds. It cannot set the price of oil.
For Ryan, that is why the path to lower yields still runs through the White House rather than Capitol Hill.Disclaimer Preview Image: Shutterstock

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) raised the reserve requirement ratio on foreign currency deposits to 6% from 4%, and the yuan weakened on the news yesterday. The PBOC announced the change at about 00:55 GMT; it takes effect on 15 November 2026 and is aimed at strengthening the management of foreign exchange liquidity at financial institutions.
Banks will have to hold more of their foreign currency deposits in reserve, which is estimated to withdraw an extra $24bn. The increase reverses a cut made in September 2023 and follows a yuan rally of more than 5% this year.
The daily fixing backed the signal. The PBOC set yesterday’s midpoint at 6.7150 per dollar, 661 pips (0.0661 yuan) weaker than the estimate and the largest weak-side deviation since 10 September 2026.

The PBOC is responding to strong market-driven yuan appreciation,

articles.title: Update: China's central bank to raise forex reserve requirement ratio to keep yuan stable - https://www.indiagazette.com/
articles.summary: Update: China's central bank to raise forex reserve requirement ratio to keep yuan stable  https://www.indiagazette.com/
articles.full_text:
Xinhua
                
03 Nov 2026, 22:14 GMT+10
            
BEIJING, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's central bank on Tuesday announced that it will raise the foreign exchange (forex) reserve requirement ratio for financial institutions by 2 percentage points, the first increase in nearly five years, in a move that is expected to ease the upward pressure on the Chinese currency renminbi and stabilize market expectations.
The People's Bank of China (PBOC) said in a statement that it will raise the forex reserve requirement ratio from 4 to 6 percent from Nov. 15 this year.
A macro-prudential management tool in the forex market, the forex reserve requirement ratio refers to the share of foreign currency deposits that financial institutions must hold at the PBOC. An increase tightens U.S. dollar liquidity and eases upward pressure on the renminbi, or the yuan, and a cut eases downward pressure on the yuan.
The latest move comes as the yuan has broadly strengthened this year. In the first nine months of this year, the yuan appreciated by a cumulative 4.2 percent against the U.S. dollar. The pace has accelerated since October, with the onshore yuan exchange rate strengthening for 14 consecutive trading days from October 14.
Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said that the increase in the ratio will help promote supply-demand balance in the forex market and curb a self-fulfilling cycle in which expectations of yuan appreciation drive further gains in the yuan.
He noted that raising the ratio is an open and transparent market-based measure, and that the adjustment sends a policy signal to the market that the central bank will stabilize market expectations and keep the yuan exchange rate basically stable at a reasonable and balanced level.
The PBOC has adjusted the ratio multiple times. In 2021, it raised the ratio twice to 9 percent. From 2022 to 2023, it lowered the ratio three times to the current 4 percent.
Following the announcement, the offshore yuan exchange rate fell against the U.S. dollar. Data from the China Foreign Exchange Trade System showed that as of 4:30 p.m., the onshore yuan spot exchange rate closed at 6.6765 against the U.S. dollar, weakening by 307 pips from the previous trading day.
In October, the PBOC issued its policy stance on the yuan exchange rate, saying that it will focus on preventing sharp short-term fluctuations in the exchange rate, especially sharp short-term depreciation that could affect financial stability.
The PBOC does not preset a target level for the exchange rate, but if the exchange rate fluctuates sharply in the short term and the market shows herd behavior and irrational expectations, it will introduce market-based measures to prevent short-term disruptive overshooting of the exchange rate, it said.
Ming Ming, chief economist at CITIC Securities, said the PBOC's move will freeze about 20 billion to 25 billion U.S. dollars of forex liquidity at the bank level and promote supply-demand balance in the domestic forex market.

articles.title: LME Week 2026: Fastmarkets Review - Fastmarkets
articles.summary: LME Week 2026: Fastmarkets Review  Fastmarkets
articles.full_text:
LME Week 2026 brought the metals industry together in London against a challenging backdrop of geopolitical tension, higher oil, freight and insurance costs, and volatility linked to a sell-off in AI equities.
In the latest Fastmarkets Fast Forward Market Briefing podcast, our experts Lee Allen, Strategic Markets Editor, Laura Roberts, Strategic Markets Editor, Julienne Raboca, Senior Price Reporter and Viral Shah, Strategic Markets Editor, discuss the conversations shaping sentiment across aluminium, copper, lithium and cobalt, and what market participants are watching as they look toward 2027.
Aluminium sentiment shifts as supply pressures ease
Aluminium emerged from LME Week with a more bearish outlook after prices moved below $3,000 per tonne, a level they had consistently traded above since the outbreak of the Gulf crisis.
The improved ability of Gulf producers to export aluminium has played an important role in changing sentiment. Material is increasingly moving into Europe, Asia and the Americas, although tensions in the Middle East and bottlenecks through the Strait of Hormuz remain obstacles.
Indonesia is also reshaping expectations. Expanding smelting capacity is bringing significant volumes into the market, with further supply expected in 2027. After a 2026 characterized by deficit conditions, market participants broadly expect a significant surplus to emerge, although uncertainty remains over exactly when that shift will occur.
Climate risks added another layer of uncertainty. El Niño-related dry conditions are already creating challenges for bauxite operations in Indonesia, including difficulties washing ore and transporting it by barge in low river levels. Similar pressures are emerging in nickel production.
Copper remains a standout despite AI volatility
Copper remained one of the most closely watched metals during LME Week. Despite already recording significant gains, it led expectations for further upside during the LME seminar.
Supply remains central to the bullish narrative, with disruptions affecting major producing regions alongside strong underlying demand. Electrification continues to support copper consumption, while the difficulty of substituting copper in many applications reinforces its longer-term demand story.
At the same time, the relationship between copper and AI has introduced additional volatility. A sell-off in AI-related equities weighed on the broader base-metals complex, highlighting how investor sentiment around AI can spill into metals markets even when underlying copper fundamentals remain unchanged.
Over the 12 months referenced in the podcast, the LME copper cash official price had risen 34%, compared with an 8% increase for aluminium.
Lithium and cobalt face bearish near-term conditions
Sentiment was markedly more bearish across lithium and cobalt, even as the underlying electrification story remained positive.
Fastmarkets’ CIF China, Japan and Korea lithium carbonate benchmark fell from around $25 per kg in May to approximately $12-15 per kg at the time of the discussion. Slower expectations for energy-storage demand growth and uncertainty about future lithium supply have contributed to the weaker environment.
Cobalt is facing its own combination of demand and supply pressures. Weakness in consumer electronics demand has coincided with rising Indonesian supply and greater availability of recycled material. This has helped offset the impact of the Democratic Republic of Congo’s export quota and intensified pressure on prices.
Fastmarkets’ cobalt hydroxide price on a CIF China basis had fallen from around $25 per lb to the mid-teens, while its standard-grade cobalt metal benchmark in-warehouse Rotterdam was just below $20 per lb at the low end of the range discussed in the podcast.
Longer term, battery chemistry is another area to watch. Growth in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and high-nickel chemistries could reduce cobalt intensity in some battery applications. But demand opportunities remain in areas requiring high-energy-density batteries, including long-range electric vehicles, drones and robotics, alongside cobalt’s established consumer electronics and alloy applications.
Metals markets head into 2027 with diverging outlooks
The discussions at LME Week point to increasingly divergent market dynamics. Aluminium faces the prospect of growing Indonesian supply and a return to surplus, while copper continues to benefit from structural demand and supply constraints.
Lithium and cobalt, meanwhile, are navigating weaker near-term pricing and rapidly changing supply and battery-chemistry dynamics.
Across all of these markets, geopolitics, climate disruption, electrification and evolving technology demand are becoming increasingly interconnected factors for participants assessing the outlook for 2027.
Listen to the full episode
Subscribe to Fast Forward, your definitive podcast for the critical minerals and battery raw materials markets. Each episode, we’re diving headfirst into the latest trends, market buzz and game-changing technologies that are shaking up this ever-changing landscape.

articles.title: China Stock ETFs Draw 472 Billion Yuan in Countercyclical Buying; Can Beijing's Policy Blitz Hold the A-Share Floor? - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: China Stock ETFs Draw 472 Billion Yuan in Countercyclical Buying; Can Beijing's Policy Blitz Hold the A-Share Floor?  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
On the afternoon of Nov. 3, China's A-share market drifted lower amid a mix of geopolitical tensions, the approaching U.S. midterm elections and an earnings vacuum, with hard-tech and dividend assets falling in tandem. Then the wind shifted near the close: several broad-based ETFs surged in volume in unison, the market's losses narrowed sharply, and the SSE 50 Index finished in the green. The Shanghai Composite and Shenzhen Component closed down 0.82% and 1.21%, respectively, while the ChiNext Index was still off 2.73% and the STAR 50 Index tumbled 3.81%. A total of 3,309 stocks across the market declined.
The force of capital positioning countercyclically through ETFs was the day's most striking signal. Six broad-based ETFs topped 10 billion yuan in turnover for the full session. The ChinaAMC SSE 50 ETF (510050) traded 12.9 billion yuan (approximately $1.9 billion), nearly four times its prior-session full-day volume of 2.6 billion yuan (approximately $389.6 million); the ChinaAMC STAR 50 ETF (588000) traded 22.5 billion yuan (approximately $3.4 billion), up from 16.7 billion yuan (approximately $2.5 billion) the day before; the E Fund ChiNext ETF (159915) traded 19.5 billion yuan (approximately $2.9 billion), versus 13.1 billion yuan (approximately $2.0 billion) previously; and the Huatai-PineBridge CSI 300 ETF (510300) traded 19 billion yuan (approximately $2.8 billion). The China Southern CSI 1000 ETF (512100) and China Southern CSI 500 ETF (510500) each also exceeded 10 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion).
Over a longer horizon, this buying support has persisted for more than three weeks. According to East Money Choice data, equity ETFs have maintained net inflows for 21 consecutive trading sessions since Sept. 28, the longest streak of daily net inflows on record, with cumulative net inflows reaching 472 billion yuan (approximately $70.7 billion). By comparison, during the sharp market correction in early 2024 (Jan. 16 to Feb. 19, 2024), equity ETFs logged 19 straight days of net inflows.
| Turnover of Major Broad-Based ETFs on Nov. 3 | Nov. 3 Turnover | Prior-Session Turnover | 
|---|---|---|
| ChinaAMC STAR 50 ETF | 22.5 billion yuan | 16.7 billion yuan | 
| E Fund ChiNext ETF | 19.5 billion yuan | 13.1 billion yuan | 
| Huatai-PineBridge CSI 300 ETF | 19 billion yuan | — | 
| ChinaAMC SSE 50 ETF | 12.9 billion yuan | 2.6 billion yuan | 
| China Southern CSI 1000 ETF | Over 10 billion yuan | — | 
| China Southern CSI 500 ETF | Over 10 billion yuan | — | 
Note: Data sourced from East Money Choice; "—" indicates the source did not disclose the corresponding figure.
On the board, computing-power hardware names led the selloff. Zhongji Innolight (300308.SZ), Cambricon (688256.SS) and T&S Communications (300394.SZ) each plunged more than 10%, while Eoptolink (300502.SZ), Shengyi Technology (600183.SS), Wus Printed Circuit (600183.SS), Dongshan Precision (002384.SZ) and GigaDevice (603986.SS) all fell. The previously defensive banking and oil sectors were not spared either: China Construction Bank (601939.SS), Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (601398.SS), Bank of China (601988.SS) and China Merchants Bank (600036.SS) dropped more than 1%, CNOOC (600938.SS) fell 3% and Sinopec (600028.SS) slipped nearly 2%.
A dense wave of policy responses was the day's other main thread. CSRC Vice Chairman Li Chao, speaking at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit in Hong Kong, said the regulator would do everything possible to safeguard the smooth operation of the capital market, steadily raise the scale and share of medium- and long-term capital entering the market, and deepen coordinated development of the mainland China and Hong Kong capital markets. A day earlier, the People's Bank of China, the National Financial Regulatory Administration and the CSRC held back-to-back symposiums and announced upgrades to two market-stabilizing structural monetary tools: the relending facility for share buybacks and increased holdings was converted from a temporary arrangement into a permanent institutional one, with its rate cut from 1.25% to 1%; and the swap facility for securities, fund and insurance companies will add participating institutions, appropriately lower swap fees and optimize collateral and operational models.
On Nov. 3 itself, the PBOC conducted 10 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion) of swap facility operations, with 31 securities and fund companies bidding and a winning rate of 10 basis points. Commitments under the buyback and increased-holding relending facility have also landed in quick succession recently, with funds explicitly earmarked for buybacks only. The CSRC on the same day adjusted and optimized rules on "market-support" buybacks, adding a stock's trading below its IPO price as one circumstance in which such buybacks may be conducted, scrapping the restriction that barred orders during the opening and closing call-auction periods for market-support buybacks, and requiring listed companies with excess fundraising proceeds to carry out buybacks promptly when market-support buyback conditions are triggered. Before the formal rule revision, regulators will support, encourage and urge qualified listed companies — especially constituents of key indices and leading tech names — to actively implement share buybacks.
The buyback market's scale has risen markedly. In the first 10 months of 2024 through 2026, the total value of buyback plans disclosed and actually implemented on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges both rose 50% from 2021-2023. In the first 10 months of this year, 645 listed companies on the two exchanges disclosed 700 buyback plans totaling 237.7 billion yuan (approximately $35.6 billion), of which 115 billion yuan (approximately $17.2 billion), or nearly half, was for cancellation; 747 companies actually repurchased 134.5 billion yuan (approximately $20.2 billion) of shares. Planned buyback value, actual repurchases, buyback-for-cancellation value and its share all hit record highs.
Separately, the PBOC announced it would raise the foreign-exchange deposit reserve ratio for financial institutions by 2 percentage points effective Nov. 15, the first such move in nearly five years, sending a clear signal of stabilizing the yuan and expectations. The CSRC's official WeChat account also published a midday rundown of its "policy combination punch to stabilize the market and expectations," responding to a cluster of market concerns.
On the outlook, institutions broadly agree short-term volatility is hard to avoid but further downside is limited. CICC said the A-share market may have already priced in overly pessimistic expectations, and that recent sustained policy signals on stabilizing growth and the market will help gradually steady investor expectations and bolster confidence; the medium-term improving trend for A-shares is unchanged.
CITIC Securities Chairman Zou Yingguang sees the market's divergence narrowing: first, a correction of overly high expectations around the tech narrative; second, capital returning to fundamentals, with the market focusing more on technology, orders and cash flow; and third, AI moving from the cloud to the edge, with the industry logic spilling over from a handful of leaders to a longer supply chain. "With divergence narrowing, given the stability and resilience of China's economy, the breadth of the A-share market is expected to keep expanding in 2027, and opportunities are accumulating," he said.
Huang Wentao, chief economist at China Securities, judges that the market has entered a bottoming zone, with three factors — regulators working in concert to steady confidence, third-quarter earnings highlights gradually emerging, and improving valuation appeal in some sectors — expected to drive an A-share bottom and recovery. Data he cited shows that as of the Nov. 3 midday close, the ChiNext Index's price-to-earnings ratio had fallen from a prior high of 53.5 times to 27.7 times, in the 6.45th percentile of the past decade, while the STAR 50's P/E had dropped from a peak of 250 times to 89 times. In his view, the valuation adjustment is creating more attractive medium- and long-term allocation conditions, and as sentiment gradually recovers, a re-matching of valuations and fundamentals could bring structural opportunities.
On the funding side, continued net inflows into ETFs — viewed as "smart money" — echo the successive escalation of policy tools. Surges in broad-based ETF volume typically correspond to passive allocation by institutions and medium- to long-term capital, and the record 21-session net-inflow streak shows some capital is absorbing market selling pressure through index products. Still, the valuation digestion in the hard-tech sector is not over: the STAR 50's nearly 4% drop on the day shows that unwinding of crowded positioning is still under way, and whether a short-term index-level recovery window opens still depends on the pace of policy implementation and the sustainability of incremental capital inflows.

articles.title: The Yuan's Strongest Stretch in Years Has China's Central Bank Reaching for an Old Tool - Trending on Weibo
articles.summary: The Yuan's Strongest Stretch in Years Has China's Central Bank Reaching for an Old Tool  Trending on Weibo
articles.full_text:
The renminbi has climbed past 6.65 to the dollar this autumn, and on Monday the People's Bank of China raised the foreign-currency reserve requirement for the first time in nearly five years to slow the rally — the same day the country's tech-heavy stock boards kept sliding.
At 8:40 on Monday morning, the People's Bank of China posted a two-sentence announcement: from November 15, the foreign-currency deposit reserve requirement for financial institutions rises two percentage points, from 4% to 6%. The tool is blunt — it locks a larger share of banks' dollar deposits away from lending — and its message is the point. It was the first time the PBoC has raised the ratio since December 2021, and it came hours after the yuan traded stronger than 6.65 to the dollar, extending a year in which the currency has appreciated roughly 4% against the greenback in the first nine months alone.
The odd thing about a strong yuan is that China's central bank treats it as a problem. Exporters earn dollars that convert into fewer yuan; expectations of further appreciation invite one-way bets, the kind of "超调" — overshoot — that the central bank's own wording signalled it wanted to avoid. Within minutes of the announcement, the offshore yuan slipped back below 6.66, exactly the response the tool is calibrated to produce.
Why the currency is strong, and why that complicates policy
The appreciation has several parents: a widening US rate-cut path, China's still-large trade surplus, and inflows betting on Chinese assets. But it lands at an awkward moment for the economy. Domestic demand remains soft, and every notch of yuan strength makes exports — one of the few engines still pulling — less competitive. Economists quoted by Chinese financial media framed the hike as "balancing foreign-exchange supply and demand," a way of buying two-way volatility rather than defending a level.
The same day carried the other half of the macro picture. Tech-heavy boards kept sliding — the ChiNext index fell about 2%, with optical-module and semiconductor names among the worst hit — extending a bruising stretch for the AI-linked trade. That decline is the domestic face of a story the site has followed already: China's tech boards ended October down more than 23% as the AI trade unwound. Retail investors' frustration was immediate — "前两天我的科技基金每天跌四五个点……平均快亏50%了," one Weibo user wrote of a fund down almost half — but the deeper signal is that money has been leaving the very sector the policy agenda celebrates, even as officials in Wuzhen opened the year's World Internet Conference pledging support for it.
The reserve-ratio hike is a modest instrument — analysts note it tightens dollar liquidity onshore rather than reversing the trend — and the central bank has other levers if appreciation pressure persists, from counter-cyclical factors in the daily fixing to guidance through state banks. But the return to a tool unused for five years marks a turning point in tone: for most of the past three years the PBoC's currency concern was depreciation and capital outflow. Managing a yuan that is too strong, too fast is a different problem — and one that says as much about the dollar's direction as about China's.

New Delhi, Nov. 5 -- Early-stage investor Jungle Ventures is preparing its next cohort of portfolio companies to go public over the coming 18-24 months. A backer of companies such as Livespace, Moglix and Turtlemint, among others, it aims to take two companies public each year, a senior company official said.
"The market has changed, and I am fortunate in that sense that in some ways our portfolio is maturing around the same time. For us, the one thing that matters is: can our companies go public? In the spirit of investing behind opportunities, teams that are going to be built to last, a big milestone or validation point is that ability to go public," said Amit Anand, founding partner and managing director, Jungle Ventures.
The firm took fintech company Turtlemint public earlier this year and has received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) for the public issue of consumer durables maker Atomberg Technologies.
"Some of our other companies such as Moglix, Livespace, Citymall, are maturing and could head towards public markets in the near future," Anand said.
The firm is currently investing from its $400-million fourth fund ($600 million including co-investment commitments from its limited partners), which it raised in 2022. Jungle Ventures has likely deployed 60-70% of this capital in India, its biggest market.
The firm is likely to close its $350-400 million fifth fund soon, with backing from International Finance Corporation (IFC), Swiss Investment Fund for Emerging Markets (SIFEM), and Asian Development Bank (ADB). Co-investment commitments from these LPs are expected to push total deployed capital past $500-600 million, taking the firm's total India investments beyond $1 billion.
The firm will focus on investing this corpus in companies spanning consumer, business-to-business, software, fintech, health-tech, and business services. It is also gearing up to hunt for investments in deeptech, manufacturing and artificial intelligence.
"I would say that for most of our earlier vintages, the majority of deals were in consumer and financial services, with 20% to 30% going into new themes each time. Sometimes it was healthcare, sometimes something else. But now we have four mainstays. Consumer and financial services are still there, but advanced manufacturing and AI have both become significant enough parts of our portfolio that they are now core pillars alongside the others," Anand said.
Jungle Ventures' track record in India includes several high-profile exits, such as the 2020 sale of mobile advertising platform Pokkt to Anymind Group and the 2015 acquisition of call-marketing startup Zipdial by Twitter. The firm also secured an exit from consumer credit platform PaySense in 2020 through a deal provided by Naspers (Prosus).
The firm writes cheques from the very early stage to early growth stages. - PRESS RELEASE
ECB wage tracker suggests slightly higher wage growth in first three quarters of 2027 compared with the full year of 2026
4 November 2026
- ECB wage tracker updated with wage agreements signed up to middle of October 2026; forward-looking horizon extended to end of September 2027
- Headline ECB wage tracker at 2.7% in second half of 2026 and 2.8% in first half of 2027; it will decline to 2.4% in third quarter of 2027 based on still-limited employee coverage
- ECB wage tracker excluding one-off payments increased from 2.6% in 2026 to 2.8% for first three quarters of 2027
The European Central Bank (ECB) headline wage tracker, which covers active collective bargaining agreements with one-off payments smoothed over 12 months, indicates negotiated wage growth of 2.3% in 2026 (based on a coverage of 46.2% of employees in participating countries). The tracker stands at 2.7% for the second half of 2026 (based on a coverage of 45.6%) and 2.8% for the first half of 2027 (based on a coverage of 31.8%), and declines to 2.4% for the third quarter of 2027 (based on a still relatively low coverage of 23.3%). The relatively low ECB wage tracker in the first half of 2026 still reflects the downward mechanical impact of one-off payments that were initially paid in the second half of 2024 and not repeated in the following year. These effects dissipate fully in the second half of 2026.
Compared with the September 2026 data release, the headline wage tracker was revised upwards slightly for the second half of 2026 and for the first half of 2027, by around 0.1 percentage points on average.
The ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments stands at 2.4% for the third quarter of 2027, down from 2.7% for the first half of 2027 and for 2026 as a whole. The wage tracker excluding one-off payments moderates to 2.5% for the third quarter of 2027 from 2.9% for the first half of 2027 and stands at 2.6% on average for 2026, continuing to indicate a limited scope for one-off payments in recently signed collective bargaining agreements. Excluding one-offs, the ECB wage tracker averages 2.8% in the first three quarters of 2027, indicating a slightly higher permanent negotiated wage growth than registered for the full year of 2026.
The headline ECB wage tracker is better suited to describing quarterly or monthly dynamics in negotiated wages as it smooths one-off payments over time. By contrast, the ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments is better suited to describing yearly dynamics in negotiated wages.
The forward-looking horizon of the wage tracker has been extended up to the end of September 2027. As new agreements are signed and coverage of contracts reaching 2027 gradually increases, the forward-looking horizon of the wage tracker will be further extended to the full year of 2027 in the December 2026 data release.
Employee coverage for 2026 stands at 46.2% but decreases significantly to 31.8% in the first half of 2027 and to 23.3% in the third quarter of 2027. The employee coverage is still limited for the third quarter of 2027 and will steadily increase over time as more wage agreements are signed. The employee coverage for 2026 and the first half of 2027 is broadly similar to that recorded at the same time last year, as indicated in the November 2025 data release. See Chart 1 and Table 1 for further details.
Overall, the ECB wage tracker may be subject to revision, and the forward-looking component should not be interpreted as a forecast, as it only captures information that is currently available for active collective bargaining agreements. Moreover, the ECB wage tracker does not perfectly track the indicator of negotiated wage growth, which is aggregated for the euro area based on country-level data on negotiated wage growth calculated by national sources (see Chart 1, left panel). Therefore, deviations from the indicator of negotiated wage growth are to be expected over time.
For a more comprehensive assessment of wage developments in the euro area, please refer to the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, which indicate a yearly growth rate of compensation per employee of 3.3% in 2026.
The ECB publishes four wage tracker indicators for the aggregate of the nine participating euro area countries on the ECB Data Portal. The data release following the December 2026 meeting of the ECB Governing Council will exceptionally be published on 18 December 2026.

The indicator of negotiated wage growth is calculated using data from the Belgian Federal Public Service Employment, Labour and Social Dialogue, the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Spanish Ministry of Labour and Social Economy, the Banque de France, the Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT), Statistics Netherlands, Statistics Austria, Statistics Finland, Haver Analytics and Eurostat.
Notes: Dashed lines denote forward-looking information (which is not yet available for the indicator of negotiated wage growth). The latest observations are for September 2027 for the ECB wage tracker indicators (left panel), August 2026 for the indicator of negotiated wage growth (left panel) and June 2027 for revisions to the previous data release (right panel).
What do the four different indicators show?
- The headline ECB wage tracker is a tracker of negotiated wage growth that includes collectively agreed one-off payments, such as those related to inflation compensation, bonuses or back-dated pay, which are smoothed over 12 months.
- The ECB wage tracker excluding one-off payments reflects the extent of structural (or permanent) negotiated wage increases.
- The ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments is constructed using a methodology that, in terms of both data sources and statistical methodology, is conceptually similar to, but not necessarily the same as, that used for the ECB indicator of negotiated wage growth.
- The share of employees covered is the percentage of employees across the participating countries that are directly covered by ECB wage tracker data. This indicator provides information on the representativeness of the underlying (negotiated) wage growth signals obtained from the set of wage tracker indicators for the aggregate of the participating countries. A recurring subplot of President Trump's term has been a desire to replace Biden appointees to the powerful Federal Reserve Board of Governors — even ahead of their terms ending — with allies. That effort now looks dead in the water.
Why it matters: Even if Trump succeeds in his efforts to fire governor Lisa Cook, or to oust any of the other three Biden-era holdovers on the seven-member board, a Democratic Senate will likely block any replacements it views as insufficiently independent from the administration.
State of play: The president seeks to fire Cook — whose term runs through 2038 — for alleged mortgage fraud, an effort that has been blocked so far by the courts. The White House plans a hearing over the allegations next month.
Former chair Jerome Powell has remained on the board as a governor, a term that ends in January 2028.
Michael Barr, whom former President Biden appointed as top financial regulator, has remained in place as a governor in a term that extends to 2032.
Philip Jefferson's term as vice chair ends this coming September, though his term as a governor extends to 2036.
Between the lines: It would break with current precedent for those officials to stick around to the end of their terms. In recent decades, Fed governor spots have turned over much more regularly, particularly after their time as chair or vice chair ends.
Powell, Barr and Jefferson may feel greater comfort relinquishing their roles as governors before the end of their terms if they are confident the Senate will block any replacements who don't respect the tradition of central bank independence.
Of note: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee that must advance Fed governor nominees, and she has assailed chairman Kevin Warsh for being a "sock puppet" of the administration.
Only one Senate Democrat, John Fetterman, voted to confirm Warsh.

Summary
- Market moving news for Asian trading on Wednesday, November 4, 2026
- Asian stocks slid as Democrats led the US midterm count, hitting AI shares: the Nikkei fell 4.4% and Kospi 3.3%. Brent oil held near $103 as Iran claimed mine strikes on four tankers near Hormuz, unconfirmed. NZ jobless rate rose to 5.7%.
Summary:
- US stock index futures fell as Democrats led the midterm count in both chambers, with S&P 500 e-minis around 7,510 and Nasdaq futures around 27,710
- AI-linked stocks led Asian losses on fears of tougher US scrutiny of data centres: the Nikkei fell 4.4%, the Kospi 3.3% and the Kosdaq 2.5%
- Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed four tankers were destroyed by mines south of Hormuz and a US MQ-9 drone was shot down. Neither claim is confirmed
- Brent traded around $103 and WTI around $96, as Iran-US talks remained stalled
- New Zealand unemployment rose to 5.7%, an 11-year high, denting the case for a December RBNZ hike
- China stepped up stock support and moved to slow the yuan’s rally, while Shanghai and Hong Kong edged lower
- BMW issued a second profit warning, Canada reported progress in US trade talks, and central bank gold buying jumped
US midterms drive risk-off move
Asian markets fell sharply on Wednesday as early results from the US midterm elections showed Democrats ahead in races for both the House and the Senate, prompting investors to dump AI-related stocks. No chamber had been formally called by late in the Asian session.
S&P 500 e-mini futures traded around 7,510 and Nasdaq futures around 27,710, with technology bearing the brunt of the selling. Traders are pricing in more friction for AI and data centre investment, along with the prospect of gridlock and drawn-out bargaining over the debt ceiling and fiscal policy if Democrats take control of Congress.
AI infrastructure became a campaign issue. The Wall Street Journal reported that voter opposition to data centres is strikingly bipartisan, though Democratic candidates have tended to be more sceptical of AI. Democratic candidates for governor in Georgia, Texas and Michigan have called for temporary bans on new data centre construction.
Japan was hit hardest in Asia, retruning from a Tuesday holiday. The Nikkei fell 4.4%, deepening losses through the session as chip equipment maker Advantest, memory chip maker Kioxia, SoftBank Group and fibre-optic cable makers came under heavy selling. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.3% and the Kosdaq 2.5%, reflecting the market’s heavy exposure to AI chips.
The selling overshadowed strong results overnight from AMD and Super Micro Computer, both of which beat forecasts and guided higher on AI demand.
Iran tensions and oil
Brent crude traded around $103 a barrel and WTI around $96, as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz intensified.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said four tankers had been destroyed and were still burning after striking naval mines south of the strait, and that two other vessels had been detained. Later, it claimed to have shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, which it said was the 56th of its kind. Neither claim had been independently confirmed.
The claims came as a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal to end their war. Tehran says the strait will stay closed until Washington waives oil sanctions, ends its naval blockade and releases frozen funds. Qatari mediators said feedback from both sides was expected within 36 hours. President Donald Trump said the US was ready to act but might have no reason to, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has hinted at an attack this week.
The US also updated its security alert for Saudi Arabia, warning of possible Houthi attacks on airports and critical infrastructure and restricting staff travel to areas including the Qatif oil region and the Yanbu export hub.
New Zealand jobs miss
New Zealand’s unemployment rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, an 11-year high, against forecasts of 5.5%. Employment fell 0.1% and wage growth slowed to 2.0% a year. The data weakened the case for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to resume rate hikes in December after its surprise hold last week, and two-year swap rates fell. NZD/USD traded around 0.560 ahead of Saturday’s general election. AUD/USD was around 0.696.
China support measures
Chinese markets were little changed, with the Shanghai Composite down 0.1% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng down 0.2%. The People’s Bank of China said applications for its share buyback loan scheme had topped 200bn yuan, after it cut the scheme’s rate to 1% and made it permanent following the CSI 300’s worst month in a decade. The central bank also moved to slow the yuan’s rally, raising banks’ foreign currency reserve requirement and setting a much weaker than expected fixing, which pushed the yuan to a two-week low. A private survey showed services activity growth slowed to a three-month low in October.
Also in focus
BMW issued its second profit warning of the year, cutting its 2026 automotive margin forecast to between minus 0.5% and plus 0.5%, citing faster job cuts, extra production costs and weak demand in China. Its third-quarter results are due on Wednesday.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said trade talks with the US would intensify, with some red lines removed and Washington asking for less and offering more, though important areas remain unresolved.
The World Gold Council said central bank gold purchases rose 42% in the third quarter, offsetting a slump in jewellery demand. It expects India’s demand to fall to a six-year low in 2026, as high prices and a weak monsoon hit buyers.

articles.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq Surge Ahead After Democratic Sweep, Dow Jumps To One-Year High On Lower Oil — AAPL, SNAP, INTC, CRWV, QCOM In Focus - TradingView

articles.full_text:
- The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 2% higher, the Nasdaq 100 rose 1%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 3%.
- Democrats won majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate.
- Oil prices dropped about 8%.
U.S. stock indices ended higher on Wednesday, with overall tech and chipmaker stocks staging a recovery as traders bet that a Democratic sweep would lead to a slowdown in AI capex and safeguard falling cash flows.
The S&P 500 ended Wednesday 2% higher, the Nasdaq 100 rose 1%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 3% to its highest level in a year. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, added 1.6%.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) rose 1.7%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) jumped 3.1%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended 1% higher on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF dropped about 3% each on Wednesday amid weakness in Nvidia (NVDA), Micron Tech (MU) and Broadcom (AVGO). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) added 0.2%.
Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for DIA improved to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’, while it remained in ‘bearish’ territory for SPY and QQQ.
US Market Drivers
| Index | Move | Close | 
| Dow Jones Industrial Average | 3% | 53,356.12 | 
| S&P 500 | 2% | 7,688.62 | 
| Nasdaq 100 | 1% | 28,437.17 | 
Traders appeared ready to shrug off political gridlock, betting that the ongoing AI boom will sustain. Analysts noted that divided government may limit additional fiscal stimulus and relieve pressure on Treasury yields, creating a favorable backdrop for equities.
“Gridlock is good,” Jason Pride at Glenmede told Bloomberg. “Markets have historically fared better when no single party can push through legislation on party-line votes. This sort of backdrop has generally been supportive for equities.”
While Democratic gains could complicate data-center development in some states, many investors see little threat to the AI investment picture. Few investors think that a Democratic win could eventually push hyperscalers to slowdown AI spending which inturn would help stop the bleeding in their cash flows.
"The blue wave will have implications for equities, with the biggest impact likely coming from an increase in data center regulation at the state level near-term," Keith Parker, UBS’s head of global macro equity strategy and US equity strategy research, wrote in a note to clients.
Furthermore, Fundstrat’s Tom Lee said in an interview to CNBC that Democratic gains in the midterms could ultimately prove positive for stocks rather than a headwind, and voiced optimism for a 15-20% rally in tech stocks.
Alternatively, Dan Ives of Yorkville Advisors, who is a well-known tech bull, anticipated a 10% to 12% correction in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) amid pressure on the tech trade following a Democratic sweep.
The Dow Jones index saw the highest gains among benchmark indices after both U.S. WTI crude and Brent crude prices dropped about 8% each.
Key Trending Stocks
Snap Inc. (SNAP) share price tumbled 11% after-hours on Wednesday after the company’s dwindling user growth offset optimism around improved financial cost structures and a better-than-expected Q4 outlook.
Apple Inc. (AAPL) is reining in employee spending on artificial intelligence, lowering daily usage caps as part of a broader corporate cost-cutting initiative, according to an exclusive report by Bloomberg.
Intel’s (INTC) chief executive officer and director Lip-Bu Tan acquired 150,000 shares of common stock worth $9.7 million on Nov. 2 via his family trust, according to a regulatory filing on Wednesday.
CoreWeave Inc.’s (CRWV) bonds as well as its share price dropped on Wednesday after a wave of Democratic wins in multiple states, including Texas, raised concerns about a slowdown in data center infrastructure builds.
Qualcomm (QCOM) announced on Wednesday that it will team up with Elon Musk’s SpaceX (SPCX) to help build Starlink’s new national cellular network.

articles.title: Trading Day: Oil tanks, stocks leap on US midterms - WTVB
articles.summary: Trading Day: Oil tanks, stocks leap on US midterms  WTVB
articles.full_text:
By Jamie McGeever
ORLANDO, Florida, Nov 4 (Reuters) – Investors put money to work on Wednesday, piling into stocks, bonds, non-dollar currencies and gold following historic US midterm elections that saw the Democrats win control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. The widespread bullishness was also fueled by a steep fall in global oil prices.
In my column today, I look at the part high inflation and the affordability crisis played in the US midterm elections, which ended in one of the biggest defeats for an incumbent Republican president in living memory.
Today’s Key Reads
• Democratic sweep adds new twist to markets’ Iran, AI, and debt worries
• Election stiffens the Fed’s guardrails, but independence risks remain
• US trade deficit narrows slightly in September; imports hit record high
• ECB rate hike looks nearly certain after inflation rises to three-year high
• Global central banks hit pause in October after September hiking spree
• Today’s Key Market Moves STOCKS: Japan -1.5%, China +2.3%. Europe +1.8%, UK +1%. Brazil +1%, snaps six-day losing streak. Nasdaq +1.4%, S&P 500 +1.6%, Dow +3%.SECTORS/SHARES: Nine sectors on the S&P 500 rise, two fall. Five sectors +3% or more, consumer discretionaries +4.2%. Energy -4.8%. Data center, defense shares fall. Big healthcare stocks post double-digit gains, but CVS -12.5%.FX: Dollar lowest since September 30. Emerging FX rallies, especially Mexican and Chilean pesos. Bitcoin +3% above $80,000.BONDS: German bund yield lowest in two months, 30-year gilt yield posts biggest fall since May, 10-year yield lowest since July. US yields down 3-7 bps across the curve.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil tumbles, Brent, WTI -8%. Gold +3.5% back above $4,000/oz, best day since August 19.
Today’s Talking Points:
Gridlock, schmidlock
Wait, aren’t political gridlock and a “lame duck” president in Washington meant to be bad news for stock markets? Not if Wall Street’s whoosh on Wednesday is anything to go by. As news of the Democrats’ “clean sweep” hit the wires late on Tuesday night, Nasdaq futures were down as much as 2.5%. The tech-heavy index closed Wednesday up nearly 1.5%, and the Dow had its best day since April last year.
As it turns out, the certainty of knowing who controls what in Washington for the next two years is rather welcome. It offers a sense of predictability, and reduces the likelihood of more radical policies being implemented. If so, the political backdrop is calmer. Also, history shows market performance in the second year of a presidential term is often weak, so the bar for recovery after the midterms is low. Will this time be different?
Game-changer oil?
We’re only at the midpoint of the week, but the plunge in oil prices on Wednesday puts Brent and WTI crude futures on course for their biggest weekly decline since the white heat of the global pandemic in April 2020. Brent is down nearly 20% so far this week, WTI is down 15%. This will cool inflationary pressures and, ceteris paribus, is bullish for stocks and bonds.
Trump admitted that the unpopularity of the Iran war was a major factor in his party’s defeat. He also said this week that the US will stop its $4 billion annual funding of Israel after this year. Meanwhile, Qatar has stepped up mediation efforts to end the US-Iran conflict. Could an end to the war finally, this time, be in sight? The oil market is trading as if it is.
Take it to the Bank
The Bank of England decides interest rates on Thursday, and is expected to finally join most of its G10 peers in raising borrowing costs to combat inflation. It would be the Bank’s first hike in more than three years. The UK already boasts the highest real rates in the G4, so a hike would widen that gap even further. Around 100 basis points of tightening is priced in by the end of next year, rates futures markets show.
Good news for sterling? Probably. The pound rose to a seven-week high against the dollar on Wednesday, and is close to testing $1.35. It is hovering around its highest level against the euro since March last year. FX strength will help cool inflation, but won’t do much to narrow the trade deficit.
What could move markets tomorrow?
• Germany industrial orders (September)
• Euro zone producer price inflation (September)
• Norway interest rate decision
• Bank of England interest rate decision
• Federal Reserve officials scheduled to speak include Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin

articles.title: ECB Succession Race Accelerates as EU Leaders Target December Choice for Lagarde Replacement - finchannel
articles.summary: ECB Succession Race Accelerates as EU Leaders Target December Choice for Lagarde Replacement  finchannel
articles.full_text:
BRUSSELS — The ECB succession process has entered a compressed new phase after European Union officials said leaders hoped to agree in December on a replacement for Christine Lagarde, who will leave the European Central Bank on Feb. 7, 2027, months before the scheduled end of her term.
Euro-area governments have been asked to submit candidates by Friday, Nov. 6. Finance ministers are due to review the process on Nov. 9, and EU leaders are aiming for a formal decision at their Dec. 17–18 summit, a senior euro-zone official told Reuters. The timetable is meant to complete the appointment before Lagarde’s departure, although several institutional consultations still stand between national nominations and a final decision.
The ECB announced on Oct. 29 that Lagarde had informed its Governing Council and European Council President António Costa that she would step down on Feb. 7. Her eight-year term had been due to end on Oct. 31, 2027. At the ECB’s monetary-policy press conference that day, Lagarde said she wanted freedom to speak and engage on matters beyond monetary policy; the bank did not offer further details about her future plans.
Lagarde’s official X account continued to publish central-bank material on Nov. 4, including an update on the ECB wage tracker. It said the tracker pointed to slightly higher wage growth in the first three quarters of 2027 than in 2026. The post was not a succession announcement. It did, however, show the ECB’s regular policy communications continuing while the appointment process is organized by EU governments and institutions outside the bank.
A short political calendar
The appointment cannot be completed through a single political endorsement. Article 283 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union provides that the European Council appoints ECB Executive Board members by qualified majority from among people with recognized standing and professional experience in monetary or banking matters. It does so on a recommendation from the Council of the EU, after consulting the European Parliament and the ECB Governing Council.
The European Council’s guidance describes the Executive Board as six members: the president, vice-president and four other members. The Board manages the central bank’s day-to-day work and implements monetary policy. Interest-rate decisions are made by the Governing Council, which includes the Executive Board and the governors of euro-area national central banks.
The immediate sequence is unusually narrow. Governments must submit candidates by Nov. 6, while finance ministers are scheduled to take stock on Nov. 9. Reuters reported that no recommendation of a single candidate was planned for that meeting unless leaders reached a political agreement rapidly. The European Parliament’s opinion is compulsory, although it does not have a veto.
Parliament is scheduled to sit from Nov. 23 to 28 and again in December. EU officials regard the Dec. 17–18 leaders’ summit as the preferred date for a formal appointment. If consultations or political negotiations take longer, Reuters reported that a January decision remains possible. Lagarde’s Feb. 7 exit is the fixed deadline in the process.
Three Board vacancies raise the stakes
The presidency is only one part of a larger turnover at the top of the ECB. Isabel Schnabel, responsible for market operations on the Executive Board, is due to leave on Jan. 3, 2027. Philip Lane, the chief economist, is due to leave when his term expires on May 31, 2027. Reuters reported that political negotiations could encompass all three senior appointments.
The vice-presidency was filled earlier this year. On March 19, the European Council appointed Boris Vujčić, the former governor of the Croatian National Bank, as ECB vice-president. The Council said the appointment followed the Article 283 process, including a Council recommendation and consultations with Parliament and the ECB Governing Council.
EU treaties do not assign Executive Board positions to particular countries. They require professional credentials, while governments commonly consider national representation, policy experience and gender balance when more than one position is open. No EU institution has announced a final package of appointments or a common candidate for the presidency.
Names in the nomination phase
The Netherlands has nominated Klaas Knot, the former governor of the Dutch central bank, Reuters reported. Spain is expected to propose Pablo Hernández de Cos, head of the Bank for International Settlements and a former governor of the Bank of Spain. The nomination period remains open until Nov. 6, and neither the Council nor the European Council has published an official shortlist.
That leaves the contest unsettled. The Eurogroup’s Nov. 9 meeting is an announced review of the process, not a selection meeting. A nominee must still receive the Council’s recommendation, be considered by the ECB Governing Council and Parliament, and be appointed by the European Council. The formal decision lies with EU leaders acting by qualified majority.
Lagarde’s decision moved the presidential choice forward. Reuters reported in September that up to two-thirds of the six-member Executive Board could change by 2027. The confirmation of a February departure moved the timetable for the presidency months ahead of the end date originally scheduled for October 2027.
What will and will not change
The succession itself does not alter ECB interest rates or create an automatic change in monetary policy. The Governing Council, rather than the president acting alone, decides policy. At its Oct. 29 meeting, the ECB held key interest rates steady at 2.5%.
The ECB said mortgage rates rose to 3.6% in August from 3.5% in July, while mortgage lending growth eased to 3.0% in September. Lagarde told the subsequent press conference that three experienced Board members would leave in the first half of 2027, identifying the institutional changes now under preparation.
On Nov. 4, Lagarde urged Europe to improve climate-related insurance, invest more in power infrastructure and help companies generate their own electricity after a summer of extreme heat, Reuters reported. She said much of that investment would need to come from the private sector and did not announce an ECB financing initiative.
Those comments were made in her capacity as ECB president, not as part of the appointment contest. The available institutional record shows two parallel processes: the central bank is publishing wage, lending and policy data, while the Eurogroup, Council and European Council prepare nominations and consultations for its next leadership.

Developments in geopolitical relations, particularly involving Iran and Ukraine, could further influence crude oil pricing. articles.full_text:
Boehringer Ingelheim has returned to China to satisfy its appetite for antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and T-cell engagers (TCEs).
In April, Paola Casarosa, Ph.D., who oversees the German pharma’s innovation unit, name-checked ADCs and TCEs as a “key focus” for the company.
“We still believe ADCs are an exciting modality,” Casarosa told Fierce at the time. “We'll continue to also look into [next]-generation payloads and new mechanisms of connecting those to the antibodies.”
Boehringer appears to be doubling down on this strategy. On Wednesday, the company announced it would pay $358 million upfront to Sino Biopharmaceutical for a six-program option and license agreement, spanning both preclinical ADCs and TCEs. Five programs come from Sino’s LaNova Medicines subsidiary, with one originating from its Beijing Tide Pharmaceutical unit.
The deal terms involve Sino overseeing early development of these assets toward agreed clinical milestones, after which point Boehringer has the option to cough up more money to license the therapies. The German drugmaker will have the chance to buy the worldwide rights for two of the drugs, and the ex-China rights for the other four.
In return, Sino could receive up to $7 billion in a combination of option-exercise fees and milestone payments, as well as tiered royalties if any of the six programs makes it to market.
Boehringer has an existing oncology partnership with Sino, which operates globally under the SBP Group brand. The German drugmaker has been established in China’s biopharma scene courtesy of its External Innovation Hub in Shanghai.
“Our second partnership with Boehringer Ingelheim marks an important milestone in SBP Group’s international innovation strategy and further validates our scientific capabilities in next-generation oncology,” SBP Chairwoman Theresa Tse said in the release.
“By combining our innovative platforms and early-development capabilities with Boehringer Ingelheim’s global oncology expertise, we aim to maximize the potential of these programs and bring innovative treatment options to patients worldwide,” Tse added. “We will continue to expand our global partner network and contribute high-quality innovation from China to global healthcare.”
Boehringer’s Casarosa said the partnership will combine the companies’ complementary scientific expertise to expand its pipeline of ADCs and TCEs.
“It puts our China strategy into action by connecting innovation from China with our global research and development capabilities,” Casarosa added in today's release. “Together, we aim to accelerate promising therapeutic approaches and create new treatment possibilities for people living with difficult-to-treat cancers worldwide.”
Boehringer has certainly been making good on its interest in cutting-edge cancer therapies. Its DLL3/CD3 T-cell engager obrixtamig is already undergoing phase 3 trials for small-cell lung cancer and extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma.
When it comes to ADCs, the Big Pharma struck a deal worth up to $991 million to license a candidate from South Korea's AimedBio last year. The company also committed around $31 million to a new R&D facility in Switzerland specifically focused on ADC development.

articles.title: Who are the frontrunners to succeed Christine Lagarde at the ECB ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - Business - Fakti.bg
articles.summary: Who are the frontrunners to succeed Christine Lagarde at the ECB ᐉ News from Fakti.bg - Business  Fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
Christine Lagarde will leave her post as president of the European Central Bank on February 7, 2027 – around eight months before the end of her eight-year term. Her early departure has opened a succession process in which economic views, national interests and the future distribution of influence in the eurozone are intertwined.
Lagarde has said she wants the freedom to speak “on non-monetary issues” and support causes that are close to her. The European Central Bank confirmed that she will vacate the post on February 7, 2027. The decision gives European Union leaders the opportunity to choose her successor before France’s 2027 presidential election.
Two leading candidates
Among the main contenders are Dutchman Klaas Knot and Spaniard Pablo Hernández de Cos. Knot, 59, was governor of the Dutch central bank from 2011 to 2025. He is associated with a tougher approach to monetary policy because of his positions during the Greek debt crisis and his criticism of the ECB’s negative interest rates.
Hernández de Cos, 55, headed the Bank of Spain between 2018 and 2024. He is regarded as representing a softer approach, but analysts cited by the Financial Times believe that the division between “hawks” and “doves” does not fully describe the flexible positions of the two candidates.
The choice, however, is not a foregone conclusion. Henry Cook, an economist at “MUFG Bank”, predicts “the usual bargaining and behind-the-scenes discussions”, stressing that frontrunners “have not always succeeded”.
The decision involves a complex vote
Eurozone countries were required to put forward nominations, and finance ministers will discuss them on November 9. To be elected ECB president, a candidate must win the support of at least 16 of the 21 eurozone countries. Those countries must represent at least 65% of the currency union’s population.
This rule allows blocking minorities to be formed. Germany, the eurozone’s largest economy, has never had one of its representatives at the helm of the ECB. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has already spoken with both Knot and Hernández de Cos, highlighting the importance of the choice for Berlin.
The change also affects other posts
The choice of president is part of a broader reshuffle in the bank’s leadership. The seat held by German national Isabel Schnabel on the Executive Board is due to become vacant, while the term of chief economist Philip Lane is coming to an end.
French President Emmanuel Macron may push for the chief economist position. This would complicate support for Hernández de Cos, as northern countries are unlikely to accept both key positions being held by representatives of Southern Europe.
If national positions block both frontrunners, negotiations could steer the choice toward a compromise candidate. The final decision will be taken by the European Council following a recommendation and consultations as part of the procedure for appointing the ECB’s leadership.

Key Moments
- USD/JPY trades just below the mid-158.00s, down about 0.20% after touching a near three-week high the previous day.
- Heightened speculation over potential Japanese intervention and renewed USD selling weigh on the pair.
- US yields ease and political uncertainty around midterm elections keeps USD bulls cautious, even as Fed expectations stay hawkish.
Pair Retreats From Recent Highs
The USD/JPY pair moved lower during the Asian session on Wednesday, reversing part of a two-day advance that had lifted it to a near three-week high the previous day. The cross came under pressure as a mix of fundamental drivers encouraged selling interest. At the time described, spot prices were trading just under the mid-158.00s, down roughly 0.20% on the day, with market participants preparing for potential volatility around US midterm election outcomes.
Intervention Risk Keeps Yen Shorts on Edge
Traders remained wary of renewed action by Japanese authorities to stabilize the Japanese Yen (JPY), curbing appetite for fresh short positions in the currency. This caution, combined with broad US Dollar (USD) softness, contributed to the downward drift in USD/JPY. Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Monday that the joint FX statement with the US persists and that the government is prepared to act to curb excessive or disorderly weakness in the JPY.
Geopolitical Optimism Pressures the Dollar
Sentiment that a diplomatic path could ease the US-Iran war further undermined demand for the safe-haven Greenback, adding to the offered tone in USD/JPY. In that context, President Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that the US has no immediate plans to strike Iran and
“we seem to be getting everything we want,”
which led traders to scale back the geopolitical risk premium and weighed on the USD.
US Yields Ease as Election Results Trickle In
US government bond yields slipped as investors tracked early midterm election developments. Markets monitored the possibility that Republicans could lose their majority in the House of Representatives and potentially in the Senate as well. The move in yields kept USD buyers on the defensive. However, expectations for a hawkish Federal Reserve limited the downside, as stronger US labor market data from Tuesday supported the case for additional policy tightening.
Labor Data and Inflation Risks Support Fed Outlook
The Labor Department’s monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) indicated that hiring remained relatively steady while job openings climbed more than anticipated in September, rising to 7.5 million from 7.2 million. At the same time, concerns over energy-driven inflation continued to reinforce expectations for further Fed rate hikes. Together, these factors argued for caution before positioning for a sustained downturn in the USD and, by extension, in the USD/JPY pair.
Rate Differentials Still Favor the Dollar
Despite the pullback in USD/JPY, the persistently wide interest rate gap between the US and Japan remained an important constraint on the lower-yielding JPY. This backdrop suggested that it may be prudent to wait for more decisive selling pressure to confirm that a near-term top in spot prices is in place. Looking ahead, traders were focused on the upcoming US ADP private-sector employment report and the ISM Services PMI later in the North American session for fresh directional cues.
Key Technical Levels for USD/JPY
From a technical standpoint, USD/JPY continued to trade underneath the 100-day Simple Moving Average (SMA) at 159.15 and the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement at 159.75. This configuration kept the short-term outlook capped and mildly bearish. The pair hovered just below the 50.0% retracement level at 158.45, highlighting this zone as an important resistance area that would need to be reclaimed to support a more durable recovery toward the upper Fibonacci band.
On the downside, initial support was seen at the 38.2% retracement at 157.16. Below that, deeper Fibonacci support levels appeared at 155.56 and close to the structural cycle low near 152.97, where demand could strengthen if renewed selling emerges.
